ann_81.original: Detects customers who make many customer-service calls and are not heavy daytime users; the model reads it as a complaint signal. Its exit (1792) is a gate on the service-call count whose threshold rises with day minutes: for the typical training customer (day minutes at the median) it is off at 3 calls (0.00) and on at 4 (1.07), largest at 5 (1.50) and falling back by 9 calls (0.42); at 100 day minutes it is on from 3 calls (0.93, and 3.72 at 5); at 300 day minutes it stays off at 5 calls (0.00) and at 9 (0.00). On the training split it acts on 351 customers, whose churn rate is 41.0% against 11.6% for the rest; through this part it adds 3.19 to the score on average for those customers (its exit feeds the output directly and, through the identity hand-off, the day-charge unit, so part of its signal is counted again there). Of the customers it acts on, 240 have 4 or more calls (out of 318 such customers in training) and 111 have 3 or fewer: light daytime users, for whom the negative day-minutes term lowers the threshold. The fall beyond 5 calls comes from the inner unit 13380, a negative feedback term that switches on at 5 calls; it rests on the 42 training customers with 6 or more calls (churn rate 66.7%), so that part of the shape is fitted to few rows. Switching the part off drops the training AUC from 0.908 to 0.813. A concept probe confirms this reading: the rule of 4 or more calls with at most 220 day minutes predicts the exit with a score of 0.98 (AUC 0.992), against 0.74 for the call-count threshold alone and 0.91 for the raw call count.
ann_81.proposed: A chain that switches on from about 4 calls to customer service for customers who are not heavy daytime users; it acts on 351 of 4000 training customers and, for a typical customer it acts on, raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 4% without it to about 90% with it. More daytime minutes lower it for those customers in an uneven way, from about 98% at 112 minutes to about 4% at 249 minutes for a typical customer it acts on (with daytime charge moved from 15.46 US dollars to 40.15 US dollars, as in the data).

ann_82.original: A hinge on total day charge (the model's second reading of daytime use) that also carries the service-call chain's output. For the typical customer with the chain off, its exit (486) is off at 30 dollars (value 0.00), on at 35 dollars (0.21) and rises linearly to 2.23 at 60 dollars; the whole-model risk of that customer goes from 2% at 30 dollars to 89% at 60 dollars (day minutes are held at their typical value in this sweep, so the day-minutes units do not move; the direct day-charge edge does). With 5 service calls (chain on), the unit is already on at 15 dollars (0.27) and reaches 3.89 at 60 dollars: the chain's output enters with a weight near one, so the service-call signal is counted a second time whenever this unit is on. It acts on 1921 training customers (churn rate 23.9% against 5.1% for the rest), adding 1.11 to the score on average for them; 1663 of those have the chain off, a pure day-charge hinge. Two small state terms (state 2 directly; state 3 through the always-on unit 14787) shift the threshold slightly for the 78 and 73 training customers in those states. parts.name: churnScore
parts.original_hypothesis: The churn score is the sigmoid of a bias plus the sum of the parts' outputs: the linear direct terms, the service-call effects (chain, its day-charge boost and the spike), the day-use shape (heavy-use hinge and the negative ramp) and the state adjustments; the parts add in the score, so their effects multiply in odds. In training the model's AUC is 0.908 and its accuracy 0.906 on 4000 rows whose churn rate is 14.1% (mean predicted risk 14.3%). The typical customer (medians; state 49, no plans, 1 service call) has a predicted risk of 2% with a score of -3.77, where the direct terms contribute 0.33 and the day-minutes ramp 0.09 relative to its mean, and the gated parts are off. Risk is driven up mainly by an international plan (direct), by 4 or more customer-service calls for customers who are not heavy daytime users (the chain, counted again through the day-charge unit) and by heavy daytime use (above about 220 day minutes, through three readings: the direct day-charge edge, the day-charge unit and the heavy-use hinge); it is driven down by a voice-mail plan and, slightly, by a few states. The 29 inputs with no enabled edge (the remaining states, area code 510, evening calls, night minutes and calls, international minutes) are unconnected and cannot move the score; they are listed as entries of this root for completeness. Fixing the direct terms at their mean drops the AUC to 0.786; switching off the chain and the day-charge unit together drops it to 0.815; replacing every nonlinear part by its best affine fit drops it to 0.834.

parts.name: directTerms
parts.original_hypothesis: The linear part of the model: a weighted sum of 35 inputs (plans, usage totals, account length and the direct state and area-code edges) entering the output through an identity node; the full sum is in the attached formula. Per standard deviation of each input, the largest edge weights include: international plan 0.79, voice-mail plan -1.13, number of voice-mail messages 0.55, day charge (its direct edge) 0.67, evening minutes 0.42, international charge 0.40, international calls -0.25, night charge 0.26, state 46 -0.27, state 11 -0.19, state 0 -0.18 and account length 0.14. In the whole model, taking an international plan moves the typical customer's risk from 2% to 26%; the 380 plan holders in training have a churn rate of 42.4% against 11.2%, and this part contributes 2.60 to their score on average. A voice-mail plan with 30 messages moves the typical customer's risk from 2% to 1% (the plan's negative weight outweighs the positive messages term); the 1061 voice-mail plan holders have a churn rate of 7.4% against 16.6%, with this part contributing -0.99 on average for them. Day charge appears here as well as in two hidden units, so its direct weight is one part of its whole-model effect. Fixing all direct terms at their mean drops the AUC from 0.908 to 0.786.

parts.name: serviceCallChain
parts.original_hypothesis: Detects customers who make many customer-service calls and are not heavy daytime users; the model reads it as a complaint signal. Its exit (1792) is a gate on the service-call count whose threshold rises with day minutes: for the typical training customer (day minutes at the median) it is off at 3 calls (0.00) and on at 4 (1.07), largest at 5 (1.50) and falling back by 9 calls (0.42); at 100 day minutes it is on from 3 calls (0.93, and 3.72 at 5); at 300 day minutes it stays off at 5 calls (0.00) and at 9 (0.00). On the training split it acts on 351 customers, whose churn rate is 41.0% against 11.6% for the rest; through this part it adds 3.19 to the score on average for those customers (its exit feeds the output directly and, through the identity hand-off, the day-charge unit, so part of its signal is counted again there). Of the customers it acts on, 240 have 4 or more calls (out of 318 such customers in training) and 111 have 3 or fewer: light daytime users, for whom the negative day-minutes term lowers the threshold. reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 26%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 2%).

The model treats a higher total daytime charge as clearly raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way: for a typical customer, it goes from about 2% at 19.07 US dollars to about 13% at 42.40 US dollars (with total daytime minutes at 236 minutes, as in the data), flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower.

The model treats a higher total daytime minutes as raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way: for a typical customer, it goes from about 2% at 112 minutes to about 11% at 249 minutes (with total daytime charge at 40.15 US dollars, as in the data), flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, the customer-service calls clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves from 4 calls upwards (for 1603 of the 4000 training customers it already changes below that): for a typical such customer, going from 0 calls to 4 calls moves it from about 2% to about 41%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.

Through one part of the model, total daytime charge clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves once it rises above about 32.37 US dollars (between 16.09 and 32.37 US dollars for different customers) (for 923 of the 4000 training customers it already changes below that): for a typical such customer, going from 0.00 US dollars to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 2% to about 13%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.
The model ignores total evening calls and total night-time calls; it does not read total international minutes and total night-time minutes itself (it reads inputs the data ties to them).
